_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 1 Computing unit lecture film, Lesson 4 Algorithm to Program. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. The chapters follow LESSON[lecture] in order (words and code; blocks; building a program; predicting; running and testing, which carries 'a computer cannot think for itself'), and close on the lesson's Programs everywhere step (1CS.05). Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The cat's positions and sizes are the lesson's own: ART.run gives the end state of every prefix of each script, so move right stopping at three and grow capping at 2.2 come from the kit and not from a copy here.
title: Algorithm to Program
subtitle: Grade 1 Computing
objectives: Know that an algorithm is a set of instructions to complete a task or to solve a problem.
Know that algorithms can be recreated as code on computers.
Know how to recreate algorithms as programs to perform simple tasks.
Predict what is likely to happen when programs are run.
Know how to run programs to test whether they produce the desired result.
Know that there are many everyday devices that use computers to control what they do.

beats.say: An algorithm is steps in words. A computer needs code.
Blocks are code. Blocks in a row are a program.
An algorithm is a set of steps in words. Move right. Jump. Say hello.

at.steps: a set of steps in words

beats.say: A computer cannot read our sentences. It needs the steps as code.
Code is instructions in a form the computer understands.
So we use blocks. One block is one instruction. Blocks are code.
Blocks in a row are a program. A program is code a computer runs.
These are the seven blocks the cat understands.
Move right slides the cat one space. Move left slides it back.
Jump makes it hop. Say hello gives it a speech bubble.
Spin turns it round. Grow makes it bigger and shrink makes it smaller.
One block does one thing. Two things need two blocks.
To build a program, read the algorithm first.
It says move right, then jump. Two steps, so two blocks.
Pick the move right block first. That is step one.
Then pick the jump block. That is step two.
The computer does the blocks in the order you place them. Match the algorithm.

at.order: in the order you place them

beats.say: Here is a program you did not build. What will the cat do?

at.program: a program you did not build

beats.say: Read every block, left to right. Do not read just the first one.
Move right. Move right again. Then jump.
Saying what will happen before it runs is predicting. Programmers do it all the time.
Now press Run. The computer does the blocks in order.
Watch the cat. Did it do what the algorithm said?
Running a program to check it is called testing.
If it did the wrong thing, change the blocks and run it again.
A computer cannot think for itself. It does what it is told.
A program does not only run on a tablet. Look around your home.
Many everyday things have a small computer inside.
A traffic light runs a program: red, then amber, then green.
A washing machine runs one too: fill, wash, spin, drain.
A robot vacuum runs a program. A game is a program too.
An algorithm in words becomes code. Code a computer runs is a program.
Build it, predict it, then run it to test it.
A computer does what your program says. Programs are everywhere.
